items.title: Assignment 4: Pipelining + Bells + Whistles
items.text:
Info

Assignment 4 involves 1 compulsory task and the rest is open-ended.

Demonstrate Post-synthesis simulation AND FPGA hardware incorporating all the mandatory and open-ended parts. Use a single assembly program that can be entirely compiler-generated, entirely handcrafted, or a combination of the two. Let your imagination run wild!

While the instructions are reasonably complete, there could still be minor updates, which will be highlighted.

items.title: Compulsory Task: Pipelining our CPU [13 points]
items.text:
Implement pipelining. Pipelining should be done such that the processor supports all the requirements for Assignment 2 and Assignment 3.

The purpose of pipelining is to increase the clock frequency. You should try increasing the clock frequency, following the tip below. For the compulsory task, it is sufficient to test and report the max frequency via CLK_DIV_BITS. There will not be additional marks for the compulsory task based on the achieved clock frequency - any attempt to increase/optimize this will be an open-ended enhancement.

Hazard hardware (forwarding, stalling, flushing, etc.) is not a compulsory task. As long as your design works with an appropriate number of nops, the requirements for this task can be met.

Tips for implementing pipelining
  • The WE of the PC given in the templates is active high, while the one given in the pipelined design (Chapter 5 (v2)) is active low. You might want to change the PC WE in the templates to active low to be consistent.
  • Even though the pipeline registers are shown as big registers storing a lot of stuff, each data stored can be thought of as being in a separate register. In other words, in your HDL code, you don't have to try and 'collect' all the bits to form a single register entity.
Increasing the clock speed

Now that you have pipelined your processor, you might be able to run it at fairly high clock speeds, especially if your program memory and data memory are small.

However, note that even with the standard 5-stage pipeline, 100 MHz (CLK_DIV_BITS = 0) may not always be achievable, especially if your memory size is large.

Up to ~430 MHz is possible, though very unlikely with a 5-stage pipeline. To increase the clock beyond 100 MHz or to attempt frequencies other than those achievable via CLK_DIV_BITS, you will need to make use of the FPGA's built-in clocking resource called MMCM (which uses phase-locked loops). This can be configured using a clocking wizard (Google for more info).

Tips for faster clock speeds:

  • Identify the bottleneck by looking at the timing report.
  • Use smaller memories.
  • For larger memories, use block ram templates (see below), and allow at least 2 clock edges, and maybe even 3 for a read. This, of course, is a major design change as the pipeline is no longer 5-stage.
  • Use a hierarchy of memories.
  • If the bottleneck is the execute stage, try to make it shorter by moving the PC logic to the M stage.

Now, how do we know what frequency it can run at? You set the clock frequency via CLK_DIV_BITS or Clocking Wizard, do synthesis and then implementation, and see the warnings. You'll get a critical warning after place and route that some timing constraints are not met if the frequency you set cannot be obtained. If you get this warning, the functionality is not reliable even if it runs on the board; frequency at which you do not get the warning is the maximum safe frequency.

To use FPGA block RAMs for instruction and data memories in pipelined version (Allows faster synthesis times and possibly clock rates for larger memory sizes): (Disclaimer: Not tested fully). Change reads to be under always@(posedge clk) where relevant. Read the comments in templates for more info. If enabled, Instr, ReadData_in are delayed by 1 cycle. Therefore, what you get can be used as InstrD, ReadDataW directly. MMIO reads are also delayed. Register file outputs are RD1E and RD2E directly if it is done for the register file.

items.title: Systematic procedure for Pipelining
items.text:
Follow these steps to implement pipelining.

  1. Start by inserting the appropriate suffixes (F/D/E/M/W) for each wire, port, register, and signal. Refer to Chapter 5 (v2) for this. For every signal that goes through multiple pipeline stages, it will need to be split into two signals, separated by a pipeline register. Note: Generally, the signals going into every component will have the same suffix, since every component is part of one and only one pipeline stage. There are some exceptions, such as the write related signals going into register file.

  2. Make the appropriate datapath connection(s) for every signal going through a pipeline register. Some connections were made implicitly, such as ALUControl. These connections will need to be made explicitly. A multiplexer must be inserted to select between PC_F and PC_E, controlled by PCSrc_E. Remember to change the datatype from wire to reg where necessary.

    • Verilog: Use a combinational always block with non-blocking assignments. For example:
    always @(*) begin
    ExtImm_E <= ExtImm_D;
end
    • VHDL: Use a concurrent statement (NOT inslude a clocked process for now). For example, ExtImm_E <= ExtImm_D; in RV.vhd

  3. Verify that your design works EXACTLY as it did previously, without any changes to the assembly language program. We have NOT yet inferred any registers, so there should not be any pipelining going on (yet!). If something has broken, now is a good time to debug it.

  4. Now, we implement the pipeline registers.

    • VHDL: Move all the signals that are supposed to go through a particular pipeline register into one clocked process in the microarchitecture (everything in one big clocked process is fine too, but it is better to keep it in separate processes for better organization).
    • Verilog: Change the combinational always @(*) to always @(posedge clk).

  5. Initialize all your signals and registers to zero. Add a condition that sets all these signals and registers to zero when RESET is asserted, and otherwise, assigns the RHS to the LHS at the clock edge.

  6. We suggest using the same clock edge for the Register file and pipeline registers, like how it is in

  7. Your processor should now be pipelined, your old program may not work as it did. You will need to add nops wherever there is any kind of hazard, to avoid these. For a start, just insert nops such that each pair of instructions having a data hazard is spaced by at least 2 instructions, for example, insert 3 nops if the two instructions are consecutive (assuming the same clock edge is used for regsiter file and pipeline registers). After each branch, insert 2 nops (or more if necessary, depending on which stage the branch is taken).

  8. Verify that your design works as it used to (it will just be slower because of all the nops).

items.title: Open-ended Enhancement [12 points]
items.text:
This is the fun part - implementing performance enhancements of your choice. There is no fixed requirement to get these points, and while we suggest some enhancements below, it doesn't mean you need to implement all (or any!) of these. Just one significant performance enhancement will suffice, and this need not be limited to the ones we have listed below. The enhancement should be over and above the compulsory task - do not implement a separate design that does not have pipelining, but has enhancements.

Hazard Hardware

This is a low-hanging fruit. It is not a very substantial enhancement in itself, but you will get some marks. Follow the design in Chapter 5 (v2). Do it systematically and incrementally, one hazard at a time, and testing via simulation at each step.

Idea: Additional instructions

You may choose to implement some additional instructions for your processor for your enhancement, or features of instructions that have not been fully implemented. The score you get for this will depend on how much additional logic you need to add for these features.

Idea: Exception handling and interrupt support

You can implement some simple interrupt handling. There is no need to conform to the RISC-V interrupt architecture.

External interrupt generation logic can be done inside the wrapper fairly easily. For example, if you want an interrupt to be raised when any of the pushbuttons are pressed, you can do interrupt = PB[3] | PB[2] | PB[1] | PB[0]. This interrupt can then be fed into the RV module from the wrapper.

Other possible exception/interrupt sources are:

  • other peripherals - e.g., counter from Wrapper
  • invalid memory address - bad_MEM_addr from the address decoder of Wrapper
  • unaligned address - easy to detect in Wrapper or RV. The additional instructions page has some info on it
  • illegal instruction - from your instruction decoder
  • division by zero - from MCycle

Some other tips:

  • You can have a hardcoded exception handler address input to the multiplexer controlling the PC input. The interrupt input itself can be used as (part of the) multiplexer select input.
  • You can write your interrupt service routine in your assembly code, figure out the starting address, and use this value as a hardcoded input to the mux. An alternative is to decide on a fixed handler address, and fill up spaces/nops in your code until the handler starts address. For example, if you fix the handler starting address to be IROM_BASE+0x100 and your 'main' program contains 30 instructions, you will need to add 34 nops before the first instruction in the handler code so that handler code will indeed be at IROM_BASE+0x100.
  • The address of the instruction that caused the exception/ that was about to be executed when an interrupt came in is saved into epc^ (exception program counter, and not ra). Since we aren't aiming for compliance, saving automatically to another general-purpose register that isn't used in your program is an option too. Saving to ra can be problematic when you have function calls as ra gets overwritten. You can then use jalr aka jr to return from an interrupt.

^ Note that epc is not a register that can be used like a general-purpose register. You need csrr to move its content to a general-purpose register. * If you wish to have vectored interrupts, you need to associate a number with each interrupt. You need a table/ROM with the starting addresses, which will be indexed by the interrupt number. The output of this ROM is to be fed into the PC multiplexer. The PC multiplexer control signal can be the logical OR of all the interrupt lines.

Idea: Branch prediction

Branch prediction is a cool feature you can implement. There are many ways to approach this; a simple scheme is explored in the lecture. More complex and advanced ones are out there, but we will not teach you about them; they're for you to discover for yourself.

Do not be afraid to go and read some research papers on branch prediction schemes. Trying to implement something from a paper that has been published can be a very rewarding and educational exercise.

Idea: Use other hardware peripherals

This is not an improvement in and of itself; however, implementing more peripherals in your design might help you better demonstrate the features of your processor.

For example, the Nexys 4 has an onboard microphone - perhaps that can be used to demonstrate DSP capabilities? RGB LEDs? VGA port? USB host? The world is your oyster.

Digilent's GitHub repository for the Nexys 4/4-DDR/A7 contains some useful code to help implement these peripherals.

items.title: Implement half-word/byte load and store
items.text:
You might want to add support for byte and half-word load and store: lb, lh, lbu, lhu, sb, sbu. This can be useful for data memory, all read-only peripherals that have meaningful bytes/half-words, and for 7-segment display.

ReadData_in is the whole word that contains the word/half-word/byte you want. You need to extract what you want, with a sign/zero(u) extension as required by the instruction. For example, when running lbu (load byte unsigned) instruction, if the last 2 bits of the address is 2'b01, and the address location specified in the instruction has 8'hAB, ReadData_in is 32'hxxxxABxx. ReadData, the word to be written into the destination register is 32'h000000AB (0s as MSBs as it is lbu). For lb, ReadData_in[15] should be replicated to the 24 MSBs. You have to do this conversion. This is better done in the W stage in a pipelined processor.

WriteData_out is a word, with word/byte/half-word aligned to where you wish to write it to within the word. The MemWrite_out bits of every byte to be modified should be 1. For example, when running sb (store byte) instruction, if the last 2 bits of the address is 2'b10 and the byte to be written is 8'hAB (or 32'b000000AB), WriteData_out should be 32'hxxABxxxx and MemWrite_out should be 4'h0100.You have to do this conversion. Another example: when running sh (store halfword), if the last 2 bits of the address is 2'b10 and the half-word to be written is 16'hABCD (or 32'h0000ABCD), WriteData_out should be 32'hABCDxxxx and MemWrite_out should be 4'h1100. You have to do this conversion.

CAUTION: Unaligned data reads and writes are NOT supported. If the instruction is lh/lhu/sh (load/store halfword), the data memory address should be divisible by 2 (the last bit should be 0) If the instruction is lw/sw, the data memory address should be divisible by 4 (the last two bits should be 0s)

Please read the relevant comments in Wrapper.v carefully.

Potential enhancement: Unaligned requests can be detected and used to generate interrupts by editing the wrapper. This interrupt could be used to do a software emulation of unaligned access via aligned access.

items.title: RV: Implement ISA extensions
items.text: See the RISC-V Specification for ideas. Floating-point, vector and cryptography are potentially interesting ISA extensions.

items.title: Design Instructions
items.text:
• All 32-bit combinational arithmetic and logical operations have to be performed inside the ALU or MCycle unit. Exceptions: + for calculating next PC, multiplication, division, enhancements such as branch prediction, a floating point unit that is distinct from ALU, etc. Pipeline hazard detection will require comparisons (for equality only) too, but they are on 5-bit values.
  • In the ALU, DO NOT use additional + signs -> this could infer additional adders. The existing addition framework should be good enough.
  • All operators are permitted on 32-bit values outside the RV module. For example, you will have to do 32-bit comparisons in the wrapper for address decoding.
  • Use of arithmetic operators:
    1. Do not use * operator. It is synthesizable, but in this course, we are implementing multi-cycle multiplication. / is not synthesizable, except on constants.
    2. All operators (including **, *, /, sll, rem, mod etc.) are allowed on constants (operations on constants are done at synthesis time, and will not infer any hardware).

items.title: Demo Program Requirements
items.text:
As before, you must write an assembly program to demonstrate the functionality you have implemented. The program must satisfy these non-negotiable requirements:

  1. The program must use at least one input and one output. Programs that simply produce outputs with no response to inputs are strictly NOT ALLOWED.
  2. The program must have some useful or interesting function, and MUST NOT be simply a testbench that produces a pass/fail message to "prove" that functions work. Such programs are great for testing, but very bad for demonstration.
  3. The program must demonstrate convincingly the specific enhancements you have made. Ideally, it should be something that would either not run at all, or run in an inferior fashion (e.g. slower) on your previously built CPU.
  4. The program must not be trivial or boring.

If your program fails to meet any of the above requirements, your demonstration will be considered unconvincing. In this case, we cannot necessarily know that your CPU actually does the things you say it does. Showing a waveform in a simulation is NOT a convincing demonstration of functionality (you can't sell a waveform to a customer buying a PC, right?). We may award as low as 0 marks for an enhancement if it is not sufficiently demonstrated with a program. Please take this part seriously and craft something interesting.

items.title: Getting to know your Nexys 4 board
items.text:
Info

This page is required reading before, or immediately after, receiving your Nexys 4 or Nexys 4 DDR FPGA board.

In this course, you will use a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) development board to learn digital design. We will loan you Nexys 4 boards; emails will be sent to inform you on how to collect the kits.

Here is the Digilent reference page for your Nexys 4, or Nexys 4 DDR. You can learn more about the specifications of the boards, and download relevant files.

items.title: Getting familiar with the board
items.text:
The large chip at the center of your board is the FPGA itself. It is the main component of the board, and indeed, the reason why it costs as much as it does. You will learn what an FPGA is in the first lab session.

The Nexys 4 boards come with a wide array of peripherals you can use to do all sorts of cool things. The simplest, and the ones we will use in this course, are the 7-segment displays (below the FPGA chip). Below the 7-segment display is an array of 16 LEDs, and below that, in turn, is an array of 16 switches. To the right of the FPGA, there are five black and two red push buttons. The black ones are designed to be general-purpose, and we can use them as inputs in our designs. The red buttons are meant to be used to reset the FPGA or a CPU design on it.

The Nexys 4 uses a micro USB connector on the top left of the board, for power, programming, and USB UART interfacing. The kits include a black cable to connect the board to your computer. It also includes a variety of other ports and connectors such as an RJ45 Ethernet jack, a VGA port and a USB port for peripherals like keyboards.

Tip

If you own a computer with only USB-C ports, then you will need an adapter. Remember to bring one with you to the labs.

The single switch at the top left of your board, between the power connector and the full-sized USB-A port, is a power switch. Slide it up to turn the board on.

items.title: Board Handling Guidelines
items.text:
Like most development boards and PCBs, your FPGA board is fragile. Treat it with care and respect, as if it were your own. It is reasonably expensive at over S$500, and not so easy to get replaced.

Here are some tips to take good care of your board:

  • Do not touch the PCB tracks, or the components on the board. Static discharge can damage or destroy electronic components, and these boards can be particularly susceptible.

  • Use the nice plastic box with foam lining to transport your FPGA board. Do not use a plastic bag or other plastic container to carry your boards, and most certainly don't put it bare in your backpack/tote/briefcase/whatever you bring to class.

  • When using the board, keep it on a stable, flat surface. Do NOT have it hanging off the USB cable, or hanging off the edge of a table, or on your lap, or anywhere that isn't a suitable, solid surface.

  • Do not leave your board inside the box while using it plugged in. Anti-static foam can be conductive and short circuit the PCB, potentially damaging or destroying your FPGA board.

  • Absolutely DO NOT DROP your board. When moving it around, hold the board by the edges and make sure the USB cable is unplugged so as to minimize strain on the port and to avoid it getting caught on something.

  • Avoid plugging and unplugging the micro-USB cable more than necessary. To reset the board, you can use the power switch on the top left of the board, or unplug the USB-A connector from your computer if really necessary. Micro USB is a notoriously fragile connector, and it's best to avoid putting more strain on it than necessary. USB-A is much sturdier so that end of the cable is not as much of a concern.

  • Apply common sense and standard practices for taking care of electronics: don't eat or drink near your board in case you get crumbs (or worse, a spill) on the board. Don't throw the board around. Plug and unplug accessories with care. Be gentle when using the switches and buttons.

items.title: Knowledge and skills expected
items.text:
This course is designed for students with a reasonably solid background in digital design and computer organization.

The official course prerequisites are CG2028 or EE2028. However, EE2026 (Digital Design) will be a strong plus, too.

If you are coming from CS2100DE - first of all, welcome back! Remembering most of CS2100DE will be more than sufficient for this course.

Preparation is the key to success

The labs for this course constitute a large percentage of your final grade (40%!), and not knowing how to design for an FPGA will make your life unnecessarily difficult.

If you haven't taken, or don't remember very well, the content from either CS2100DE or EE2026 - we highly, highly, highly recommend (did I mention we highly recommend?) working through the manuals for labs 1 through 4 from CS2100DE. We recommend working through these in the first 3 weeks of the semester, before starting the CG3207 labs.

If you are an official student for the course, drop the teaching team an email, and we will do our best to let you borrow a Nexys 4 FPGA board early, so you can work through the aforementioned labs.

items.title: Hardware required
items.text:
For this course, you will need an FPGA development board. We will provide you a Nexys 4 board, and our materials will expect you to use this specific board. You will also need a Windows or Linux (preferred) computer to run the software to program this FPGA. The PCs in the lab will have the software required for this course installed for you, and you may use these as well.

Note

If you are not an official student of this course, and do not have access to a Nexys 4 board to follow along, you can use any other Xilinx/AMD FPGA development board, like the Basys 3 or Arty A7. You may need to make some changes to your code and project files to account for the different FPGA and different available peripherals. You may also be able to use a completely different brand of FPGA, like an Intel or Sipeed board. However, you will not be able to use Vivado, nor our template files.

The FPGA board comes with a USB type A to USB micro-B cable. You will need a USB type A port on your laptop, and if you do not have one, you must use an adapter. Remember to bring one to class.

items.title: Software required
items.text:
The software you will use to program your FPGA board is Vivado. Installation instructions can be found here. Please install Vivado before coming for your first lab in Week 4.

To explore RISC-V assembly, we will use the RARS architecture simulator. This runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and does not require any installation and can be run by double clicking the downloaded jar file or by running java -jar filename.jar where filename is the name of the jar file you downloaded.

items.title: Installation Guide for Vivado
items.text:
Warning

Please note that this is the CG3207 website. If you are taking a different course, you may have been directed here for the instructions to install Vivado.

Please DO NOT get confused, and start doing the labs for CG3207, if you are not taking CG3207.

For this course, we recommend using Vivado 2023.2. Any other version of Vivado you have installed will probably work; however, you will need support for 7 series FPGAs to be able to use the Nexys 4 board.

Note

Vivado runs on Windows and Linux, but not on macOS. However, we have recently found that it is possible to run Vivado on a Mac computer using Parallels Desktop. Our test setup was as follows:

  • MacBook Pro with M1 Max CPU
  • macOS Sequoia version 15.4
  • Parallels Desktop Pro version 20.2.2, running Windows 11

Download and install Parallels Desktop. Create a virtual machine for Windows 11 on Parallels Desktop, then in that VM, follow the steps for Windows in this guide. To successfully connect your FPGA board to Vivado, you will need to install the latest version of the Digilent Adept Runtime, as the cable drivers included with Vivado may not install correctly.

If you are an NUS student, you may obtain a license for Windows 11 Education from here.

We have not (yet) tested Vivado running on a Linux VM (e.g. Ubuntu on Parallels), or using other hypervisors (e.g. VMWare Fusion, QEMU etc.). These setups may work, but are not guaranteed to do so. We understand Parallels Desktop is paid (and not cheap) software, so if you are unable to obtain a license to use it, we recommend either borrowing a laptop/PC from someone you know, or using the lab PCs which have the software preinstalled.

Download Vivado from AMD/Xilinx's website. We echo AMD's recommendation to download the web installer instead of the full, 100+ gigabyte archive. Download the exe or bin file, depending on your operating system of choice.

You will need to create an account to download Vivado and fill out a form for US export control regulations. You will also need to enter this information when you install the software.

items.title: Windows
items.text: You should be running Windows 10 or 11. Xilinx recommends the Pro or Enterprise version of certain specific versions of Windows; however, Vivado runs just fine on any version of 10 or 11. Simply open the downloaded executable file. Make sure you allow it through your firewall when prompted, and note that it may show up as "OpenJDK Platform Binary" executable requesting permission.

items.title: Linux (Ubuntu, RHEL, etc.)
items.text:
To install Vivado on Linux, you may first need to install some dependencies. On Ubuntu, these are libtinfo5 and libncurses5. Install these with sudo apt install libtinfo5 libncurses5. Some googling will find you the equivalent packages and commands for other distributions like Red Hat/Fedora and Arch. Xilinx officially supports some specific versions of RHEL, CentOS, SLE, Amazon Linux, AlmaLinux and Ubuntu; however, Vivado will probably run on other distributions like Fedora or Arch.

Additionally, for Linux, the installer will not automatically install cable drivers for you. After you install Vivado, you must follow the following steps:

# change directory to your Vivado install, for example:
cd /opt/Xilinx/Vivado/2019.2

# cd into the drivers directory (the script MUST be run there)
cd data/xicom/cable_drivers/lin64/install_script/install_drivers

# run the cable installer with root privileges
sudo ./install_drivers
These steps can also be found on Xilinx support.

To run the installer, first use chmod u+x filename.bin to add execute permissions to the downloaded bin file. Remember to replace "filename" with the name/path of the downloaded file. Run it using sudo ./filename.bin.

items.title: Next Steps
items.text: You may wish to see the Getting Started manual which teaches you some of the basics of how to use Vivado and Verilog to create a design for an FPGA.

items.title: Demonstrations
items.text:
Small, self-contained programs showing why memory access patterns, data layout and parallelism dominate performance, plus two Verilog snippets showing what synthesis tools do to your RTL. The source files are in the Demonstrations folder of the course repository. All examples are AI-generated; absolute timings depend on your machine, but the ratios are what matter.

Contents

  1. Background: caches and hardware prefetching
  2. Prefetching experiment (cache_access.c)
  3. Other CPU memory-layout examples
  4. Parallel / GPU examples
  5. Verilog / Yosys examples
  6. Number representation demos
  7. Quick reference

Build tip: compile with -O2 for meaningful timings. Files using clock_gettime may need -lrt on older glibc (harmless on newer).

items.title: 1. Background: caches and hardware prefetching
items.text:
Modern CPUs move memory in cache lines (typically 64 bytes = 8 doubles). Two rules explain almost every result below:

  • The cache line is the unit of transfer. Order within a line is irrelevant; what matters is how many distinct lines you touch and in what order.
  • Hardware prefetchers watch your access pattern and fetch lines before you ask for them, turning "compulsory" misses into hits.
Prefetcher Detects Example Sequential / stream consecutive lines 100, 104, 108 → fetches 112, 116… Stride constant stride 100, 200, 300 → learns +100, fetches 400, 500… Next-line (always) fetches the line after the current one

Caveats: prefetchers operate between lines, not within them; they do not cross page boundaries (1–4 KB); and prefetched lines can evict useful ones.

items.title: 2. Prefetching experiment (cache_access.c)
items.text:
Traverses a 64M-element double array (~512 MB) in six orders. A "block" is 64 elements (~512 B, ~8 cache lines).

# Pattern Cache Prefetcher Expected 1 Perfect sequential: 0 1 2 3 … excellent spatial locality stream prefetcher runs far ahead best 2 Fully random every access misses nothing to learn, stays idle worst 3 Sequential inside block, blocks in random order good within a block, miss at each block start random jumps defeat it moderate 4 Random inside block, blocks random same as #3 same as #3 = #3 5 Sequential inside block, blocks at constant stride (3) good stride prefetcher learns block order (0→3→6→9→1→4…) very good 6 Random inside block, blocks at constant stride (3) same as #5 same as #5 = #5

Key insights

  1. The cache line is the fundamental unit for both caching and prefetching.
  2. Order within a line is irrelevant, which is why 3≡4 and 5≡6.
  3. Regular strides are prefetchable even when not sequential.
  4. Prefetching turns caching from reactive (fetch on miss) into predictive (fetch before use), but only when the pattern is learnable at cache-line granularity.

Run 

gcc -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer cache_access.c -o cache_access
./cache_access

Sample output (one machine; needs ~1 GB RAM) 

1) Perfect sequential:                             0.131 s
2) Fully random:                                    0.857 s
3) Block-seq inside, block-random:                 0.146 s
4) Random-in-block, block-random:                  0.131 s
5) Block-seq inside, constant-stride blocks:        0.107 s
6) Random-in-block, constant-stride blocks:         0.107 s
Note #5/#6 beat even #1 here, and random is ~6–8× slower than everything else. The "dummy sum" printed at the end only prevents the compiler from deleting the loops.

items.title: col_row_maj_cache.c: row-major vs column-major traversal
items.text:
Sums an N×N matrix (default N = 3000) two ways: row-major (for i { for j }, sequential) and column-major (for j { for i }, stride N). Each is timed REPS = 100 times; only the average is printed. Column-major is typically ~5–6× slower with far more cache misses. The sum is stored in a volatile sink so -O2 cannot remove the loop.

gcc -O2 -o col_row_maj_cache col_row_maj_cache.c -lrt

./col_row_maj_cache            # both (default)
./col_row_maj_cache -r         # row-major only
./col_row_maj_cache -c         # column-major only
./col_row_maj_cache -n 5000    # matrix size (a bare number also works: -c 5000)
./col_row_maj_cache -h         # help

# Compare cache misses, one pattern per run
perf stat -e cache-misses,cache-references ./col_row_maj_cache -r
perf stat -e cache-misses,cache-references ./col_row_maj_cache -c
perf stat --repeat 5 -e cache-misses,cache-references ./col_row_maj_cache -c   # steadier
If perf reports "No supported events found": sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1 (or use sudo). Counts include the identical init phase, so the difference comes from the traversal. Sample (N = 3000, -O2): Row-major average time: 0.012 sec, Column-major average time: 0.070 sec. A full run takes a few seconds (~1 s row, ~7 s column).

items.title: aos_vs_soa.c: Array of Structures vs Structure of Arrays
items.text:
Sums only the x field of 64M particles {x,y,z,w}. With AoS, 75% of every fetched cache line (y/z/w) is wasted; with SoA, x values are contiguous, so SoA is significantly faster. 

gcc -O2 -o aos_vs_soa aos_vs_soa.c -lrt
./aos_vs_soa

items.title: matrix_transpose_optimization.c: pre-transposing B
items.text:
In C = A×B, the naive loop reads B[k*N+j], striding by N each step. Transposing B once lets the inner loop read B_T[j*N+k] sequentially, so both operands stream through the cache. SIZE = 1024. 

gcc -O2 -o matrix_transpose_optimization matrix_transpose_optimization.c -lrt
./matrix_transpose_optimization

items.title: matmul_comparison.c: six matrix multiply variants (1024×1024)
items.text:
Progressively applies optimizations and times each (also prints threads available and a first-element check that all results agree):

  1. Standard (poor locality for B)
  2. Transposed B
  3. Blocked (tiled)
  4. OpenMP parallel
  5. "SMT-aware": parallel + transposed + blocked (block 64)
  6. "NUMA + SMT aware": per-thread init, dynamic scheduling, block 128

Speedups vary with core count, cache sizes and NUMA topology. 

gcc -O2 -fopenmp -o matmul_comparison matmul_comparison.c
./matmul_comparison
OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 ./matmul_comparison     # control thread count

items.title: gpu_demo.c: GPU (OpenCL) vs CPU
items.text:
Runs a 1024×1024 matrix multiply and a 10M-element vector multiply on both. Matrix multiply gains far more from the GPU because it is compute-bound (O(N³) work on O(N²) data); element-wise vector multiply stays memory-bound (O(N)), so the GPU helps little once transfer costs are counted. 

# Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt-get install ocl-icd-opencl-dev   (plus a GPU/CPU OpenCL runtime, e.g. pocl-opencl-icd)
gcc -O2 -o gpu_demo gpu_demo.c -lOpenCL
./gpu_demo
Prints CPU time, GPU time and speedup for each operation, then a summary.

items.title: 5. Verilog / Yosys examples
items.text: These show how many flip-flops synthesis actually produces. Requires Yosys.

items.title: dff_infer.v / dff_infer_keep.v: duplicate registers
items.text:
Two 8-bit registers (reg_a, reg_b) share the same clock, synchronous reset, enable and data_in, so the RTL implies 16 flip-flops. Yosys sees they are always identical and merges them:

Stage Result FFs after proc $dff_8 ×2 16 proc; opt $sdffe_8 ×1 (reset/enable folded in, duplicates merged) 8 generic synth $_SDFFE_PP0P_ ×8 8 synth_xilinx -family xc7 FDRE ×8 (+1 BUFG, 0 LUTs) 8 dff_infer_keep.v (* keep *) blocks the merge 16

stat -width prints cell width as a _8 suffix, so cells × width = flip-flops. In Yosys 0.33 the (* keep *) must be on the always block; on the reg declaration alone it is not enough.

yosys -s dff_infer.ys       # reports all five stages
# or manually:
yosys -p "read_verilog dff_infer.v; synth -top dff_infer; stat -width"
yosys -p "read_verilog dff_infer_keep.v; synth -top dff_infer; stat -width"

items.title: multiplication_optimisation.v: constant multiplication folds to a shift
items.text:
result = data_ext * (12'd13 + 12'd3). The constants fold to 16 during elaboration, so synthesis replaces the multiplier with a fixed left shift by 4: no $mul cell survives, and the output is just wiring. Writing the same arithmetic as two terms, (data_ext * 12'd13) + (data_ext * 12'd3), is not folded by Yosys, and the hardware cost jumps:

Stage data_ext * (13 + 3) (data_ext * 13) + (data_ext * 3) coarse synth -run coarse (RTL cells) 0 cells 1 × $macc generic synth (gate level) 0 cells ~170 gates (exact count varies with Yosys version) synth_xilinx -family xc7 I/O buffers only, 0 DSP48E1, 0 LUTs 2 × DSP48E1

multiplication_optimisation.ys runs all three stages on the current RTL; edit the assign line to try the two-term form.

yosys -s multiplication_optimisation.ys
# or manually:
yosys -p "read_verilog multiplication_optimisation.v; synth -top transfer; stat"

items.title: 6. Number representation demos (number_formats.c)
items.text:
Four short predict-observe-explain demos in one program. For each one: write down your prediction, press Enter, then compare with the output and explain any difference. Demos 1 and 3 are meant to surprise you.

gcc -o number_formats number_formats.c
./number_formats        # all four demos, in order
./number_formats 3      # just demo 3 (valid: 1-4; anything else prints usage and exits 1)
# Demo What it shows 1 Bits inside a float (-9.875f, read via a union) Prints 0xC11E0000; work out sign, exponent and mantissa 2 8-bit fixed point (int8_t, value = int / 128) 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 truncate to 12, 25, 38, so (a + b) - c is -1, not 0 3 16-bit fixed point (int16_t, value = int / 256) A * B for 1.5 * 1.5 overflows int16_t (result 0.25, not 2.25); fix with a 32-bit intermediate, then >> 8 4 Float addition order a = 1e30, b = -1e30, c = 1: (a + b) + c is 1 but a + (b + c) is 0. volatile stops the compiler folding the sums

items.title: Interactive visualisations
items.text:
Browser-based simulators for topics from the lectures. Each one runs a small example cycle by cycle, so you can see what the hardware or software is doing at every step, and change the parameters to see what that does to the result. Each has a short guide with suggestions for what to try.

Simulator What you can explore Guide Cache Run an access trace through a cache of your choosing. Compare direct-mapped, set-associative and fully associative mapping; LRU, FIFO and optimal replacement; write-back and write-through. Each miss is classified as compulsory, capacity, conflict or coherence. cache.md Interrupts Raise an interrupt and follow it through the context switch, the ISR and the return, in vectored and non-vectored mode. interrupt.md Multithreading Two threads on one superscalar core under no multithreading, coarse-grained, fine-grained, barrel and SMT policies. See which issue slots go unused and why. multithread.md Data parallelism The same loop on scalar, SIMD and SIMT hardware. Warp divergence, latency hiding through warp scheduling, and memory coalescing. dataparallel.md Systolic array Matrix multiplication on an n × n array, output-stationary and weight-stationary (TPU-style). Fill and drain time, PE utilisation, operand reads. systolic.md OpenCL One OpenCL host program from device discovery to read-back, with work-groups executing on compute units. opencl.md

items.title: Cache memory simulator: user guide
items.text:
cache.html is a single self-contained file (CSS and JS inline). Open it in a browser; no server or other files needed.

It runs a trace of memory accesses through a configurable cache, one access at a time: mapping, replacement, write policies and the types of misses.

items.title: Addresses
items.text:
Byte addressing is the default: 4 bytes per word, so the address has two byte-offset bits below the word field. Word addr drops them. Switching keeps the memory size (address bits change by 2) and rewrites the trace addresses, so the same locations are accessed and the results do not change.

Fields, high to low: tag, index, word, byte. The index is called Block for a direct-mapped cache and Set otherwise; a fully associative cache has none. Memory block number = address ÷ block size.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
Control Sets Address bits Width of the address, hence memory size Words/block, Cache blocks Cache geometry Mapping Direct mapped, N-way set associative, fully associative Replace LRU, FIFO or Optimal. Hidden when direct mapped Writes Write-back (dirty bit, whole block written on eviction) or write-through (every write goes to memory). Both allocate on a write miss

The examples run one trace under direct, 2-way and fully associative mapping, a reference string for each replacement policy, a miss-type example, write-back against write-through, and a DMA invalidation.

items.title: Trace
items.text: One item per access: R addr, W addr, or D addr (a DMA write to that block in memory). A bare number is a read. Decimal, 0x hex and 0b binary are accepted; items can be separated by spaces, commas or new lines; # or // starts a comment. Set Numbers are to block numbers to type a reference string such as 1 2 3 4 1 2 5. Press Run or Ctrl+Enter after editing.

items.title: Reading the results
items.text:
Each miss is classified as:

Type Rule used Compulsory First reference to the block Capacity A fully associative LRU cache of the same size would also miss Conflict That cache would have hit Coherence The block was invalidated by DMA since it was last fetched

The Replace panel runs FIFO, LRU and Optimal on the same trace and geometry, one column per access showing the accessed set afterwards, f for a miss. It appears only when there is a replacement choice. Optimal breaks ties by evicting the lowest-numbered way.

In the cache table, recency #1 is the most recently used line (LRU), age #1 is the oldest fill (FIFO), and next use is the access number at which the block is next needed (Optimal). A struck-through tag is a line invalidated by DMA.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
Control Action ▶ / → Next access ◀ / ← Previous access ⏭ / End Last access ⏵ / Space Auto-play (speed selector beside it) ⟲ / R / Home Back to the start Slider, trace row, comparison column Jump to that access

On a phone the Lookup, Cache, Replace and Trace panels are tabs; the controls stay on screen.

items.title: Data parallelism: user guide
items.text:
dataparallel.html shows the same data-parallel work on different hardware, one cycle per step. It covers SIMD/vector versus SIMT, warp divergence and latency hiding, plus memory coalescing as the next question on GPUs.

Open the file in a browser. It needs no server, but dataparallel_engine.js must sit in the same folder.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
Control Action ▶ / Space Play or pause ▶| / → One cycle forward ◀ / ← One cycle back ⏮ / Home Start 1 to 4 Switch demo Slider Scrub to any cycle

Each demo keeps its own position and settings. Changing a setting rewinds that demo. On a phone, Setup shows the settings.

items.title: 1. SIMD · SIMT
items.text:
y[i] = a*x[i] + y[i] on a scalar core, a vector core and a SIMT core. Each issues one instruction per cycle.

  • Elements and Lanes set n and the vector or warp width. Pick an n that is not a multiple of the width to see the tail: the last strip or warp leaves lanes idle, and "lanes busy" drops below 100%.
  • The vector core runs vsetvli plus four vector instructions per strip. The SIMT core runs four per warp and masks the threads past n.
  • Set lanes to 1: the vector core is slower than scalar, because it still pays for vsetvli.

items.title: 2. Divergence
items.text:
One or more warps run if (x[i] > 0) A else B. Every lane evaluates the condition, then each path runs with the other lanes masked off. A path no lane takes is skipped.

  • Data order sets the signs of x. With 50% taken, sorted by sign keeps whole warps on one side and nothing diverges, while random splits almost every warp.
  • Click a data cell to flip that lane.
  • Path A and Path B set the instruction counts. "Independent lanes would need" is the cost if each lane followed its own path.

items.title: 3. Latency
items.text:
Warps share one core. Each issues a burst of instructions ending in a load, then waits. The core keeps issuing from a warp while it can, otherwise switches to the next ready warp.

  • With the defaults (4 warps, bursts of 2, latency 6) the core never idles, so latency is fully hidden.
  • Reduce Resident warps until idle cycles appear. Warps needed is ⌈(burst + latency) / burst⌉.
  • Warp 0 finishes no earlier than it would alone. Only the total time improves.

items.title: 4. Coalescing
items.text:
One warp loads a word per lane. Memory is served in aligned segments, one transaction per cycle, so the cost is the number of segments touched.

  • Compare a[i], a[i+1] (misaligned), a[s*i] and a[idx[i]].
  • Segment sets the transaction size. A stride of at least the segment size costs one transaction per lane.
  • The readout names the vector load that does the same job: vle32.v (unit stride), vlse32.v (strided), vluxei32.v (gather).

items.title: Simplifications
items.text:
• One instruction issues per cycle and every instruction takes one cycle, except the loads in demo 3 and the transactions in demo 4.
  • Loop control, address arithmetic and the bounds check are not counted.
  • Demo 3 has one scheduler and no limit on registers. On a real core, the register file bounds the resident warps.
  • A transaction in demo 4 is one segment per cycle with no caches.

items.title: Files
items.text: File Role dataparallel.html Page: tabs, rendering, transport. dataparallel_engine.js DOM-free models for the four demos, loaded by the page and the tests. dataparallel_tests/engine.test.js Results and invariants for every demo. node opencl/dataparallel_tests/engine.test.js dataparallel_tests/ui.test.js Drives the page in Chromium at desktop, phone and dark settings. NODE_PATH=$(npm root -g) node opencl/dataparallel_tests/ui.test.js dataparallel.md User guide.

items.title: Engine
items.text:
Each function simulates a demo up front and returns plain data; the page replays it one cycle per step, so scrubbing needs no state reconstruction.

  • axpy({n, w}): instruction records for a scalar, a vector and a SIMT machine over y[i] = a*x[i] + y[i]. A record is {line, kind, group, lanes[], vals[]}; lanes[j] is the element lane j works on or -1. yAt replays the stores.
  • Scalar: 4 instructions per element. Vector: vsetvli plus 4 per strip, vl = min(w, n left). SIMT: 4 per warp, threads past n masked.
  • Lane utilisation counts the vector instructions only: n / (w * ceil(n / w)).
  • diverge({w, warps, pattern, p, seed, costA, costB, flips}): per warp, one compare, then path A if any lane takes it, then path B if any lane does not. The taken count is exact (round(p * lanes)), placed by a seeded shuffle, sorted order or alternation. "Independent" cost is 1 + max(path cost) per warp.
  • latency({warps, issue, lat, rounds}): a warp issues issue instructions per burst; the last is a load that stalls it lat cycles, except the final burst, which ends in a store. The scheduler stays on the current warp while it is ready, otherwise takes the next ready warp in round-robin order. Grid cells are I issuing, M waiting, R ready, D finished. Speed-up is measured against running the warps one after another.
  • coalesce({w, seg, pattern, stride, seed}): addresses from one of six patterns, grouped by floor(addr / seg); one transaction per distinct segment, issued in address order. Efficiency is distinct words over words fetched.

items.title: UI rules
items.text:
• Transport, narration and settings live in the header, so the controls stay on screen while the result scrolls. The narrow layout (≤ 860 px) hides settings behind Setup and keeps the four demos as one row of tabs.
  • Only the active view is in the DOM.
  • Each demo is a function of (model, k), rendered in full on every step.
  • All sizes are in rem; the root font size is clamp(13px, 1.05vw, 28px). Row and cell heights in demos 3 and 4 also scale with viewport height, so a projected page fills the screen. Settings share the title row on wide screens, which saves a header row, and the narration is a banded block.

items.title: Interrupt simulator: user guide
items.text:
interrupt.html compares vectored and non-vectored interrupt handling on a RISC-V core, one step at a time. A main loop runs until you raise an interrupt from one of two peripherals; you then step through the context switch, the interrupt service routine (ISR) and the return.

Open the file in a browser. It is a single self-contained file (CSS and JS inline) and needs no server.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
Control Action Click Peripheral 1 or 2 Raise that IRQ. Only accepted while the main program is running ▶ / → / Space Next step (clicking anywhere on the page body outside a button also steps) ◀ / ← Previous step (the last 50 are kept) ⟲ / R Reset Vectored / Non-Vectored buttons Switch mode; this also resets

The state banner shows the current phase and mode. The register panel shows PC, EPC (the saved return address) and the IRQ ID of the interrupt being served.

items.title: The two modes
items.text:
Vectored Non-vectored Entry PC loads the handler address from the vector table, indexed by the IRQ PC always loads the one common handler at 0x9000 Finding the source Done by hardware: each IRQ has its own table entry Done by software: the handler reads INT_STATUS and branches with bne Handler ack_int_n, work, eret Polling code, then jal to a per-peripheral routine, ret back, eret Extra display Vector table, with the selected entry highlighted Polling indicators for peripherals 1 and 2

Steps in a vectored interrupt:

  1. Main running: PC walks the four-instruction loop at 0x0000 to 0x000C.
  2. Interrupt pending: you clicked a peripheral; its IRQ line lights up.
  3. Context switch: the vector table entry for that IRQ is highlighted.
  4. ISR running: EPC now holds the interrupted PC and PC points into the handler. ack_int_n clears the IRQ line.
  5. Interrupt return: eret copies EPC back into PC and the main loop resumes where it left off.

Non-vectored mode skips the context-switch step: the next step after the interrupt goes straight to 0x9000 with EPC saved. The polling code checks peripheral 1 first, then peripheral 2, so the handler for peripheral 2 runs after one extra failed comparison.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• In vectored mode, raise IRQ 2 and count the steps from the click to the first instruction of its handler. Repeat in non-vectored mode and compare.
  • In non-vectored mode, raise IRQ 1, then IRQ 2 in a second run. Watch the extra bne that the second one needs, and which line each ret returns to.
  • Step back from the eret and watch EPC and PC to see exactly what is restored.
  • Try to raise a second interrupt during an ISR. It is ignored: the simulator handles one interrupt at a time.

items.title: Simplifications
items.text:
• One interrupt is served at a time. There is no nesting, priority, masking or mstatus/mcause registers, and no pending queue.
  • The simulator shows a program-level view. Instructions are not decoded or executed: lw, addi, sw and the rest only advance PC, and ack_int_n is a pseudo-instruction that clears the IRQ line.
  • jal/ret in the non-vectored handlers follow fixed addresses rather than a real link register.
  • There are no tests for this page.

items.title: Hardware multithreading: user guide
items.text:
multithread.html runs the same two instruction streams on one superscalar core under five policies, one cycle per step.

Open the file in a browser. It needs no server, but multithread_engine.js must sit in the same folder.

items.title: Reading the picture
items.text:
Columns are cycles and rows are issue slots. Blue instructions belong to thread A (hart 0) and orange to thread B (hart 1); the number is the instruction's position in its thread. A red hatched slot is lost because no thread could issue that cycle. A dashed slot is unused in a cycle where something did issue (the thread had no more independent instructions). A purple hatched slot is a pipeline refill after a coarse-grained switch.

An M on an instruction is a load that misses in the cache; the thread then stalls. A d is an instruction whose result the next instructions need, which costs a one-cycle bubble. The two strips under each grid give each thread's state every cycle: solid is issuing, striped is waiting on a miss, dotted is waiting on a dependency, and an outline is ready but not picked. This is what explains the schedule: when one thread issues alone, the other's strip is striped or dotted. A refill slot is labelled with the thread it switches to. Hover any slot for the reason.

All four rows share one time axis, so a scheme that finishes sooner simply ends sooner.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
Control Action ▶ / Space Play or pause ▶| / → One cycle forward ◀ / ← One cycle back ⏮ / Home Start Slider Scrub to any cycle

Changing a setting rewinds. Reshuffle draws new instruction streams. On a phone, Setup shows the settings and the grids shrink to fit; instruction labels and badges are hidden and a missing load is a dark-outlined block.

items.title: Schemes
items.text: Scheme Rule What it hides None Run A to the end, then B. Nothing. Coarse-grained Run one thread until it stalls on a cache miss, then switch (refill cost). Long stalls only. A one-cycle dependency stall is not worth a switch. Fine-grained: barrel Strict rotation: even cycles belong to A, odd cycles to B, ready or not. Stalls shorter than the rotation. A stalled thread's turn is wasted, even if the other thread is ready. Fine-grained: skipping A different ready thread every cycle; a stalled thread is skipped. Short and long stalls. SMT Both threads can fill the slots of one cycle. Stalls, and unused slots when one thread lacks ILP.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Issue width is the number of slots per cycle.
  • Thread ILP is the most independent instructions a thread can offer in a cycle. Groups are one to that many instructions.
  • Stalls sets how often a group is followed by a one-cycle dependency stall or a cache miss. Miss latency is the length of a miss.
  • Switch cost is the refill, in cycles, paid at each coarse-grained switch.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• In fine-grained, thread A issues alone in cycles 5 to 8. Look at B's strip: B4 missed, so B waits until cycle 11 and the core takes the only ready thread.
  • Compare the barrel with the skipping fine-grained row. In the barrel, cycle 6 is B's turn and B is waiting on its miss, so the cycle is lost although A is ready. Skipping uses it for A. Defaults: 28 cycles against 23.
  • With the defaults the finish times are 40, 30, 28, 23 and 20 cycles. Compare the red and dashed slots row by row: skipping fine-grained and SMT lose the same whole cycles, and SMT recovers the partly empty ones.
  • SMT's lead over fine-grained is biggest when one thread cannot fill the width. At width 4 with ILP 1 or 2 it is about 2.5 cycles on average; at width 2 with ILP 2 or more a single thread nearly fills the core and the lead shrinks to under one.
  • Raise the switch cost from 0 to 3 with many stalls and a miss latency of 8. Coarse-grained slows from about 47 to 59 cycles, while fine-grained stays at 45. Switching is cheap per stall only if the stall is long.
  • Compare "A done" across rows. Thread A finishes at cycle 20 on its own, 22 under fine-grained and 24 under coarse-grained. Each thread gets slower; the pair finishes sooner.
  • Raise the miss latency to 12. Even fine-grained and SMT lose many whole cycles, because two threads cannot cover a miss that long. GPUs keep many warps resident for this reason.

items.title: Simplifications
items.text:
• The core issues in program order within a thread. A group of instructions is independent; the next group waits for the stall after the previous one.
  • A thread has no more than one outstanding stall, and switching never loses a thread's registers (each hart has its own copy).
  • Fine-grained, both kinds, issues from one thread per cycle but can issue up to the full width from it. Once a thread has finished, the barrel serves the remaining one every cycle.
  • SMT alternates which thread gets first pick of the slots each cycle.

items.title: Engine
items.text:
MT.run({width, ilp, stalls, lat, switchCost, groups, seed}) generates two instruction streams and simulates each of the five policies to completion. Every policy sees the same streams.

  • Streams: a list of groups of independent instructions. A group has 1 to ilp instructions. After each group except the last there is a stall: none, a one-cycle dependency stall, or a miss of lat cycles, with probabilities from the stalls preset. A group may issue across several cycles when slots run short; the stall counts from the cycle after its last instruction.
  • None: thread 0 to the end, then thread 1.
  • Coarse-grained: run one thread until it is stalled on a miss and the other is ready, then switch and pay switchCost refill cycles (all slots lost). A thread that finishes also hands over. One-cycle stalls never trigger a switch.
  • Barrel: strict rotation. Cycle t belongs to thread t mod 2 whether or not it is ready, and all width slots go to it. When a thread has finished the barrel serves the other every cycle.
  • Fine-grained (skipping): each cycle the next ready thread after the last issuer, else the same one; all width slots go to that thread.
  • SMT: each cycle the threads alternate who picks first; the first fills what it can, the second takes the remaining slots.
  • Causes: the last instruction issued from a group carries the group's stall kind (miss or dep). Each cycle also records every thread's state: run if it issued, otherwise its stall kind while readyAt is in the future, wait if ready but not picked, done once finished. A lost cycle always has a stalled thread; a refill cell records the thread it switches from and to.
  • Slot accounting: a slot is an instruction, a refill, lost in an empty cycle (vertical waste) or unused in a busy cycle (horizontal waste). They sum to width × cycles, and the instruction count is the same under every policy.

The default seed is chosen so the four policies finish in clearly different times. The tests check program order, stall respect, one thread per cycle for the non-SMT policies, that the barrel only issues in its own turn, that the skipping policies and SMT never lose a cycle while a thread is ready (the barrel can), refill accounting, and the ordering none > coarse > barrel > fine ≥ SMT averaged over 60 streams (a single stream can break it: a switch cost can make coarse-grained slower than the baseline).

items.title: UI rules
items.text:
• All sizes are in rem with the root font size clamp(13px, 1.05vw, 28px); cell height also follows the viewport height so the five cards fit a 1080p screen.
  • All four grids share one time axis. Above 860 px each grid scrolls horizontally if it needs to and follows the current cycle; at or below 860 px every cycle is fitted to the width, instruction labels are hidden and the ruler shows every fifth cycle.
  • Stall causes are drawn three ways: a badge (M, d) on the instruction, two thread-state strips under each grid, and a tooltip on every slot. Under 860 px the badges and labels are hidden (a missing load keeps a dark outline) and the strips remain.
  • Transport, narration and settings sit in the header, so the controls stay on screen while the cards scroll.

items.title: OpenCL in action: user guide
items.text:
opencl.html steps through one complete OpenCL host program: platform and device discovery, buffer transfers, the kernel launch, work-groups running on compute units, and the read-back. It follows the 13 execution steps of a typical OpenCL host program and a main.c example.

Open opencl.html in a browser. It needs no server or install, but opencl_engine.js must sit in the same folder.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
Panel Shows Code main.c and kernel.cl. The current host call is highlighted; a red highlight means the host is blocked in that call. During the kernel, the kernel line being executed is highlighted too. Platform Host memory, the PCIe link, and the device inside its context: objects, command queue, global memory, the work-group scheduler, and each compute unit with its local memory and PEs. NDRange Every work-item, coloured by work-group. Click one to inspect it. Work-item / Traffic The selected work-item's get_*_id values, where it runs, and its private memory; bytes moved at each memory level so far.

On a phone the panels are tabs, and the kernel/device settings sit behind Setup.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
Control Action ▶ / Space Play or pause ▶| / → One step, animated ◀ / ← One step back ⏭ / Shift+→ Skip to the next host call or work-group round ⏮ / Home Start 1 to 13 Jump to that step of the list. Steps 5 and 6 come after 7 and 8, because main.c calls them in that order. Slider Scrub to any step

Each step's badge shows which memory level it touches (private, local, global, PCIe). Steps that touch slower memory play for longer. The timing is relative, not cycle-accurate.

Particles show data moving: purple over PCIe, blue to or from global memory, green to or from local memory, amber for commands and work-group dispatch. Cells outlined in blue are being read and cells outlined in orange are being written. A coloured bar under a data cell marks the work-group that owns that element.

items.title: Kernels
items.text: Kernel Shows vec_add The standard example. One work-item per element: two global loads, an add in private memory, one global store. invert A 2D NDRange over an image, get_global_id(0) and (1). 32 × 32 with 8 × 8 local shows the work-group tiling clearly. reduce_sum Local memory and barrier(). Each work-group sums its slice in __local scratch, and the host adds the per-group results.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Change the global size, local size, number of compute units and PEs per CU to see how the work is scheduled. Only local sizes that divide the global size and fit the maximum work-group size (256) are offered; the reduction also needs a power of two.

  • More work-groups than CUs: the groups run in rounds, and the last round may leave CUs idle.
  • More work-items per group than PEs: the group runs in waves. With reduce_sum, work-items that reach a barrier wait there until later waves catch up.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• Set vec_add to 64/8 with 4 CUs, then change to 1 CU. Nothing about the result changes, only the number of rounds.
  • In reduce_sum, step through the s loop and watch the active lanes halve each iteration. Compare global memory traffic with vec_add: the partial sums stay in local memory.
  • Pick a work-item in the NDRange and follow its private variables as it runs.

items.title: Simplifications
items.text:
• Each compute unit holds one work-group at a time, and a group's waves run one after another. Real devices keep several groups resident and interleave waves to hide memory latency.
  • All CUs step in lockstep, so rounds are uniform.
  • The device is generic: its compute units and PEs are the ones in the settings.

items.text: File Role opencl.html Page: layout, rendering, animation, controls. opencl_engine.js DOM-free trace generator, loaded by the page and by the tests. opencl_tests/engine.test.js Results and execution-model invariants over every offered configuration. node opencl/opencl_tests/engine.test.js opencl_tests/ui.test.js Drives the page in Chromium at desktop and phone widths. items.title: Engine
items.text:
OCL.build(cfg) simulates the whole host program up front and returns steps[]. cfg = { kernel, gsz:[x,y], lsz:[x,y], cus, pes }. Each step carries:

  • phase (0 to 13, the host program step numbering) and chapter (one host call or one work-group round, used by ⏭).
  • host / kern: line tags to highlight. Host code is generated per kernel with tags attached to lines, so highlighting never depends on line numbers.
  • ops: primitive state mutations (halloc, copyHG, gset, lset, pset, wi, wg, qpush, cnt, ...).
  • flows, reads, writes: what moved where, for particles and cell outlines. leg 0/1 splits a step into a read half and a write half.
  • lanes: {cu, pe, wi, active, note} for execution and barrier steps.

stateAt(k) clones the nearest checkpoint (every 32 steps) and replays ops, so scrubbing backwards is cheap.

items.title: Execution model
items.text:
• Work-groups are dispatched round-robin: group g runs on CU g % C in round floor(g / C). One group per CU at a time.
  • A group of L work-items on P PEs runs in ceil(L / P) waves; work-item ll runs on PE ll % P in wave floor(ll / P).
  • The kernel is a list of segments separated by barriers. For each segment, each wave runs every statement in it, then reaches the barrier. The barrier releases after the last wave arrives.
  • A statement's active predicate masks lanes (divergence). Masked lanes still occupy the step.
  • All busy CUs execute the same statement in the same step.
  • Global and local reads of never-written cells throw, so a trace that reads undefined data fails to build.
  • Local memory is allocated at dispatch and freed when the group finishes.

items.title: Relative latency
items.text: Animation duration = 650 ms × factor ÷ speed. Factors: host 0.6, private/ALU 0.7, control 0.9, local 1.0, global 1.9, PCIe 2.4.

items.title: UI rules
items.text:
• The narrow layout (≤ 860 px) turns the panels into tabs. Transport and narration stay fixed in the header, so the controls are always on screen with the result.
  • Animated steps scroll the Platform panel so that the particle endpoints are visible; if they don't all fit, the destinations win.
  • Values that don't exist yet are not drawn: unwritten cells are blank, the NDRange is hidden until step 10, and private variables show — until assigned.
  • Numeric arrays of the same shape in host and global memory share one cell size, so corresponding elements line up.
  • All sizes are in rem. The root font size is clamp(13px, 1vw, 26px), so a 1080p projector gets about 1.5× the laptop scale. Canvas cell caps, the cell font and particle radius multiply by SC() (root font size / 13) to follow it.
  • At 1080p the Platform panel fits the host, device and four compute units without scrolling; the three arrays of a memory sit in one row and the Platform column takes the largest share of the width.

items.title: Systolic array: user guide
items.text:
systolic.html runs a matrix multiply on an n × n systolic array, one cycle per step. It covers the array at the heart of the TPU and the classic output-stationary diagram.

Open the file in a browser. It needs no server, but systolic_engine.js must sit in the same folder.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
Control Action ▶ / Space Play or pause ▶| / → One cycle forward ◀ / ← One cycle back ⏮ / Home Start Slider Scrub to any cycle

Changing a setting rewinds. Reshuffle draws new matrices. On a phone, Setup shows the settings.

items.title: Dataflows
items.text:
Output stationary Weight stationary (TPU) Stays in the PE The running sum of one element of C One weight Moves right Elements of A Elements of A Moves down Elements of B Partial sums Setting Inner dimension K Rows of A streamed Cycles K + 2(n − 1) n (load) + rows + 2(n − 1)

Inputs enter skewed by one cycle per row and column, so matching elements meet in the right PE. The zeros beside the array are that skew. A PE multiplies only when both of its inputs are present, so a diagonal wavefront of busy PEs sweeps across the array.

items.title: Things to try
items.text:
• Output stationary, 4 × 4, K = 4 is the classic diagram. Step to cycle 4: ten PEs are busy. Step on and watch P11 finish first and P44 last.
  • Raise K. Fill and drain cost the same 2(n − 1) cycles however long the stream, so "PEs busy" climbs towards 100%.
  • Switch to weight stationary and watch the weights load, then stay fixed. Stream 4 rows, then 16: the fill and drain are amortised over more results.
  • Read "Operand reads from the buffer". Each input enters at an edge once and is reused by a whole row or column of PEs, so the count is n times smaller than for a MAC unit that fetches both operands for every multiply. This is the "no access to memory during each operation" point.
  • At 256 × 256 and 700 MHz (the first-generation TPU) the array does 65,536 MACs per cycle, about 92 trillion operations per second counting a multiply and an add separately.

items.title: Simplifications
items.text:
• Every PE does one multiply-accumulate per cycle, and values move one PE per cycle.
  • Weights load by shifting one row per cycle from the top. The real TPU double-buffers them so the next tile loads while the current one computes.
  • Matrix entries are small integers; there is no 8-bit saturation, accumulator width or activation unit.
  • The array is square and the matrices are sized to it. A larger matrix would be tiled.

items.title: Engine
items.text:
SA.run({mode, n, len, seed}) simulates the whole multiply up front and returns frames[0..cycles]; frames[t] is the state after t cycles. The page renders a frame as a pure function of k, so scrubbing needs no replay.

A frame holds pe[i][j] (a, b, ps, w, acc, active, final, plus the k index each operand carries), the upcoming values on each edge (qL, qT, including skew zeros), the cumulative MAC count and, for weight stationary, the rows of C emitted so far.

  • Output stationary: C = A (n × len) · B (len × n). Row i of A and column j of B enter i and j cycles late. PE (i,j) multiplies the operands on its left and top inputs when both are present, adds to its own sum and forwards both. It is busy during cycles i + j to i + j + len − 1. Total len + 2(n − 1) cycles.
  • Weight stationary: C = A (len × n) · W (n × n). Load phase of n cycles: row n − 1 − l of W enters the top on cycle l and shifts down, so W sits in place afterwards. Compute phase: A's column i enters row i i cycles late and moves right; PE (i,j) adds a · W[i][j] to the partial sum from above and passes it down. C[r][j] leaves the bottom of column j on compute cycle r + j + n − 1. Total n + len + 2(n − 1) cycles.
  • Utilisation is n² · len / (n² · cycles), counting load cycles. Operand reads count each input once at its edge (2·n·len, or n² + n·len with the weights), against 2·n²·len for a MAC unit that fetches both operands per multiply.

The tests check the result against a direct matrix product, the busy window of every PE, that each multiply pairs matching k and each partial sum extends the same row, that weights never move during compute, and the classic 4 × 4 case (10 cycles).

items.title: UI rules
items.text:
• Transport, narration and settings live in the header, so the controls stay on screen while the result scrolls. On the narrow layout (≤ 860 px) the settings sit behind Setup, and PE cells shrink rather than scroll.
  • Matrices A, B/W and C sit beside the readouts. C fills as sums become final (output stationary) or as rows leave the array (weight stationary).
  • All sizes are in rem; the root font size is clamp(13px, 1.1vw, 30px). The PE grid is sized from its container with container query units (--pe is the smaller of the width and height budgets, minus the queue gutters), so it fills the card at any screen size, and PE text scales with --pe. Matrices switch to a compact style when either side exceeds 8, so A, B and C fit in one row beside the array.

items.title: UART Details
items.text:
In the following lines, 'read's and 'write's are from the perspective of the RISC-V processor (assembly language program), and act as 'console in' and 'console out' respectively.

  • Read from the UART_RX only if the LSBit of UART_RX_VALID is set. Similarly, write to the UART_TX only if the LSBit UART_TX_READY is set (not very important if the processor runs on a slow clock).
  • Successive writes to the UART (sw / STR followed by sw / STR, i.e., consecutive sws / STRs in your assembly language program) are not supported. Similarly, successive reads (consecutive lws / LDRs) are not supported.
  • Allow sufficient time for the program to read a character before sending the next character from RealTerm. Any character received while one character is waiting to be read would be ignored. This shouldn't be a problem if your processor runs at high speed (CLK_DIV_BITS is low).
  • There is one holding register and no FIFO. uart.vhd does not buffer, and the single byte is held in TOP_Nexys.vhd. A character arriving while one is unread is discarded, and the earlier one is kept. No status bit records this.
  • At 115200 baud a character takes 10 bit-times, i.e., 8640 clocks of the 100 MHz clock (86.4 us). With CLK_DIV_BITS = 5 the processor runs at 3.125 MHz, so a character is 270 instructions. Your polling loop has to read within that.

  • Reading UART_RX when UART_RX_VALID is 0 returns 0 and does not consume anything.

  • A 32-bit number can be sent as hexadecimal in ASCII format (8 characters), which will require some processing in your program before it can be used as a 32-bit operand (note : '0' is 0x30 and 'A' is 0x41 in ASCII). It is a good idea to echo characters so that you can check whether UART has received it correctly. Also, note that backspace doesn't work to 'delete' the sent characters unless you implement such a functionality explicitly in your assembly language program.

  • If you use a console, some parts of your program could be repetitive, best implemented using a subroutine. A subroutine is normally implemented using a BL/jal instruction which we have not implemented. A workaround can be seen in the HelloWorld program for Lab 2.

  • In the simulation with UART, setting radix to ASCII could help.

  • Read the instructions in Wrapper.v/vhd before using it.

items.title: Realterm - Terminal for UART
items.text:
Realterm is an amazing serial monitor program, which could be very useful. You can use this for sending and receiving data through the UART console. Teraterm (used in EE2028) is fine too, just that RealTerm is TeraTerm on steriods. RealTerm needs .NET framework to be installed.

Note : The baud rate used depends on the baud rate set in TOP.vhd. In the template provided, it is 115200.

Figure 1(a) and 1(b) : Screenshot illustrating RealTerm settings.

RealTerm allows you to send and display data that is not necessarily ASCII. Sending and receiving raw bytes can be very useful. In fact, it is THE most effective way to get data in/out of the system.
